illustrations.alt: A small mobile group has paused on a wind-exposed river terrace. One adult strikes a stone core beside flakes; another lifts heated river stones with wooden tongs from a shallow fire; two others sort plant foods and repair a light hunting point. No large kill is staged.
illustrations.caption: Open the archaeological sequence with a materially credible Upper Paleolithic camp rather than a generic mammoth hunt. The image establishes mobility, stone procurement, cooking, cold-period vegetation, and the uncertainty of clothing and shelters.

illustrations.alt: At the mouth of a shallow rock shelter, a hunter quietly fits a small stone point to a light wooden shaft while another checks a simple bowstring. A younger person returns with a hare and a few birds; deer tracks cross damp ground beyond.
illustrations.caption: Show the Mesolithic transition through one observable hunting episode: lighter projectiles, smaller game, a rock-shelter base, and a warming forest. This avoids presenting bow adoption as a single miraculous invention.

illustrations.alt: Near a cave mouth, one adult supports a small round-bottomed vessel in soft earth beside a low fire while another crushes and adds fibrous plants. A third person prepares clay coils and presses a simple raised ridge into the surface.
illustrations.caption: Make the earliest pottery materially intelligible as small, fragile, low-fired vessels used in a marginal southern environment, while distinguishing secure objects from uncertain invention narratives.

illustrations.alt: A household-sized group works on higher ground above an inward-moving bay. Two people gather oysters and clams at the tidal edge; others tend an outdoor hearth beside three small pit dwellings and upright pointed vessels. A small dog sniffs among discarded shells.
illustrations.caption: Establish the first coastal communities through a small settlement, shifting shoreline, shellfish collection, dogs, and pointed vessels, without turning the scene into a large mature Jomon village.

illustrations.alt: During a light rain, residents repair a drainage ditch around one low pit dwelling while another household opens only the top layer of a leaf-lined nut storage pit. Smoke escapes from an interior hearth; the shared center remains open and trampled.
illustrations.caption: Show the Early Jomon shift toward durable domestic space: houses arranged around an open center, interior hearths, drainage, storage pits, and flat-bottomed pottery.

illustrations.alt: On a damp riverbank platform, one person hollows and smooths a wooden bowl with an adze, another weaves a reed basket, and a third applies a thin red lacquer layer to a comb beneath a small shelter. Nearby, gourds, nuts, fish, and cordage are being sorted.
illustrations.caption: Reveal the breadth of Early Jomon material life at a waterlogged site: woodworking, basketry, lacquer, fishing, plant foods, and possible tending of useful plants.
illustrations.confidence: HIGH for objects; MODERATE for scene

illustrations.alt: In early autumn, several households process chestnuts and acorns around a spring-fed village. One person leaches bitter nuts in running water, another carries a basket from the forest, and a family works around a central hearth inside a round pit dwelling.
illustrations.caption: Present the Middle Jomon highland florescence as an integrated seasonal system of springs, nut processing, obsidian routes, substantial houses, and the central hearth.

illustrations.alt: A highland potter builds a thick-walled Katsusaka jar with modeled ridges while a visitor or exchange partner unwraps a smaller glittering mica-tempered Otamadai vessel. Nearby, a second worker incises a rim and another tends an open firing bed.
illustrations.caption: Show Middle Jomon pottery variation and exchange through skilled work rather than isolated hero objects. The image contrasts highland Katsusaka forms with mica-tempered Otamadai vessels without pretending both were made by one identical community.

illustrations.alt: At the edge of a communal work area, an older adult holds a clay figurine over a folded hide while another person uses a stone to break one limb deliberately. Fragments from earlier acts lie sorted in shallow baskets; two observers prepare a small lamp and ordinary vessel.
illustrations.caption: Represent Jomon ritual through an observable act—handling and deliberate breaking of clay figurines—without inventing doctrine, supernatural energy, or a formal priesthood.

illustrations.alt: After prolonged rain, residents remove hearth stones and useful timbers from a damp, partly abandoned house. Others bind baskets and carry tools downhill along a muddy track; rotten nuts and waterlogged storage show ecological stress without melodrama.
illustrations.caption: Visualize the contraction of the highland world without depicting a single catastrophic collapse. The scene emphasizes repeated wet seasons, failed storage, dismantling, and movement toward lower valleys.

illustrations.alt: In spring, a dugout canoe returns through shallow water with fish while people on the mudflat gather shellfish. On the terrace, others open clams, mend nets or lines, and smoke fish; a hunter repairs a simple bow away from the main group.
illustrations.caption: Show Late Jomon seasonal coastal life through coordinated but non-specialized marine work: clamming, canoe return, fish processing, hunting gear, and restrained pottery.

illustrations.alt: People arrive in small groups at one concentric stone circle during a cool autumn gathering. Some carry baskets of salmon and nuts; others place or adjust small stones at a radial setting. A burial or offering is suggested only by a covered shallow pit, not shown explicitly.
illustrations.caption: Represent the Oyu stone circles as a carefully built communal landscape connected to gathering and exchange, while avoiding an unsupported astronomical ceremony.
illustrations.confidence: HIGH for layout; MODERATE for activity

illustrations.alt: Beside a wet disposal and working area, two specialists apply red lacquer to a wooden comb and a basketry vessel while others polish small bowls and inspect a hollow figurine. Finished objects dry under a shaded rack away from dust.
illustrations.caption: Show the technical assurance of northern Latest Jomon craft through red lacquer on wood, basketry, and household vessels, with ritual objects present but not dominating.
illustrations.confidence: HIGH for objects; MODERATE for workshop

illustrations.alt: Adults and a child work barefoot in a small irrigated paddy beside the Mikasa River. One uses a wooden rake, another sets stakes and clears a shallow water channel, while people on firmer ground carry harvested wild plants, fish, and grain toward a mixed working area with Yusu and early Yayoi pottery.
illustrations.caption: Make the Jomon-Yayoi transition visible as mixed production rather than abrupt replacement: wet paddy work, older pottery traditions, stone tools, wooden implements, gathering, and maritime influence.
illustrations.confidence: HIGH for paddy and tools; MODERATE for people and superstructure

illustrations.alt: At the edge of a defined cemetery, four adults carefully lower a large joined jar burial into an angled pit while a child watches from beside smaller single jars. Nearby rectangular pits and a covered wooden coffin area show varied burial forms.
illustrations.caption: Show the agricultural community's distinct cemetery and the practical, socially meaningful labor of jar burial without sensationalizing the dead.
illustrations.confidence: HIGH for burial forms; MODERATE for ceremony

illustrations.alt: A burial party prepares an extended east-oriented grave in sandy ground. In the middle distance, a small central stone cist receives jasper and shell ornaments, while simpler graves extend outward with fewer goods.
illustrations.caption: Visualize emerging social difference through cemetery organization, body orientation, central cists, and selective ornaments rather than by inventing a king or noble court.
illustrations.confidence: HIGH for grave arrangement; MODERATE for social reading

illustrations.alt: A craft group shapes a long granary slat and a wooden rake. One worker uses a small iron-edged adze mounted in a wooden handle; another planes a board; a smith at a tiny sheltered hearth reheats and repairs an edge rather than smelting ore from scratch.
illustrations.caption: Show how scarce iron transformed work by enabling precision in wood, while avoiding an unsupported large iron industry or a simple 'Iron replaces wood' narrative.

illustrations.alt: After heavy water flow, villagers repair a breached paddy bank and clear a wooden sluice. Others carry grain toward a raised storehouse, inspect a well, and stabilize posts around a shallow oval house.
illustrations.caption: Depict mature Yayoi collective management through an ordinary irrigation repair at Toro, integrating paddies, ditches, houses, raised storage, flood risk, and shared labor.
illustrations.confidence: HIGH for site plan; MODERATE for living scene

illustrations.alt: At dawn after an alarm, residents carry grain jars toward deep storage shafts while others repair a ditch and extinguish a small house fire near the enclosure edge. Two armed lookouts watch the route below; no battle is underway.
illustrations.caption: Show conflict as a pressure on settlement form, storage, and community obligation rather than as a cinematic battlefield.

illustrations.alt: A team prepares to pour a small bronze bell or weapon form. Two heavy stone mold halves are aligned in a shallow working pit; one worker operates bellows while another steadies a small crucible with wooden and clay supports. Finished pieces and failed cast fragments are few and scattered.
illustrations.caption: Make bronze production physically credible: heavy molds, alloy preparation, bellows, risk, flaws, and specialist cooperation. The image separates craft evidence from later political interpretation.
illustrations.confidence: HIGH for molds and debris; MODERATE for furnace arrangement

illustrations.alt: On a wooded ridge, a group lowers several bronze bells and ceremonial halberds into a prepared pit lined with mats. Others carry additional objects uphill wrapped in fiber cloth. The deposit is orderly but not yet fully covered.
illustrations.caption: Show public surrender of scarce metal through a plausible burial act at Sakuragaoka, while leaving motive—offering, concealment, boundary rite, or periodic retrieval—unresolved.
illustrations.confidence: HIGH for objects; MODERATE for deposition scene

illustrations.alt: Inside a large but non-palatial compound, Himiko sits partly screened in a dim inner space with several female attendants. Her brother or male intermediary receives tribute bundles and relays words to visitors in an outer area guarded by armed men. Himiko is seen in profile or three-quarter shadow, not as a definitive portrait.
illustrations.caption: Offer a cautious reconstruction of Himiko's authority from contemporary Chinese testimony: seclusion, female attendants, armed guards, and a male intermediary. It must not become an authentic portrait or fantasy queen scene.

illustrations.alt: A small migrating war-band pauses at a mountain pass after failing to enter the Kinki directly. The leader later called Jimmu kneels with companions near a simple offering of food and branches while scouts study the eastern route. No kami is shown physically.
illustrations.caption: Represent Jimmu as retrospective court memory rather than documentary history. The image shows ritualized travel and consultation in a plausible late Yayoi landscape while visibly avoiding supernatural proof or an authentic portrait.
illustrations.evidenceBasis: RETROSPECTIVE TEXTUAL + LITERARY OR MYTHIC + ARCHAEOLOGICAL SYNTHESIS

illustrations.alt: On a steep south-facing slope, coordinated workers place uniform bronze swords in four ordered rows within an oblong pit. A cloth or mat covering is being drawn over completed rows; a second small team prepares bells and spearheads at a nearby spot.
illustrations.caption: Present Izumo's material power through the extraordinary ordered deposition at Kojindani, while refusing to identify the actors with mythic rulers or to treat the cache as a direct illustration of Okuni Nushi.
illustrations.confidence: HIGH for arrangement; MODERATE for deposition action

illustrations.alt: Hundreds of workers are not shown; instead, a manageable section of a vast earthwork is under construction. Teams carry baskets of soil up temporary ramps, compact a terrace, set wooden markers, and coordinate drainage around the developing keyhole-shaped mound. The full outline is only partly visible from a nearby rise.
illustrations.caption: Close the chapter at the threshold of the Kofun age by showing the new scale of coordinated labor and monumentality in the Nara basin, without identifying a specific tomb occupant or turning construction into royal propaganda.
illustrations.confidence: HIGH for mound form and scale; MODERATE for construction scene

sections.title: Court Memory and the Peoples Before Yamato

paragraphs.text: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki begin the human history of the archipelago with a conquest remembered from the viewpoint of the later Yamato court. Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, later called Jimmu, moves from southern Kyushu toward the Yamato plain with selected clan leaders and meets resistance at every stage. Some opponents submit after their chiefs are killed, while others are represented as physically strange, socially deficient, or scarcely human. The Tsuchigumo, or earth spiders, occupy the lowest place in this hierarchy, and later rulers are credited with completing their destruction.

paragraphs.text: These stories are not contemporary reports of a securely dated migration. They are retrospective court traditions that distinguish a divinely favored line from the peoples it claimed the right to command. Their argument is not that the future rulers came first, but that creation, divine counsel, and demonstrated worth entitled them to rule. Even so, the memory of resistance preserves a political truth in altered form. The archipelago was inhabited by many communities before one coalition began the long centralizing process that produced the Yamato kingdom.

paragraphs.text: The earliest Chinese historians called the inhabitants of the islands Wo, or Wa in Japanese pronunciation, and described numerous organized communities rather than one state. Yamatai appeared among them as the strongest political center known to the continental record. Wa was an external category, perhaps disparaging, while people within the archipelago probably identified themselves through settlements, landscapes, occupations, kin groups, and local polities. Names such as Kumaso, Emishi, Nakatomi, and Imibe belong to different kinds of identity and to different stages in the formation of recorded society.

paragraphs.text: For periods without contemporary writing, these differences must be reconstructed through material remains. Pottery, stone tools, dwellings, skeletons, burial practices, food systems, and settlement patterns reveal changing ways of life, though their archaeological labels were not names used by the people themselves. The broad movement runs from mobile Paleolithic bands, through more settled Jomon communities supported by hunting, fishing, and gathering, to Yayoi societies shaped by rice agriculture, metallurgy, hierarchy, and ritual rule. This was not the unfolding of a nation already present in embryo. It was the long convergence of regional societies.

paragraphs.text: The islands of Japan are the exposed heights of the eastern Asian continental shelf. During colder phases, lower sea levels opened routes across ground later covered by water, while warming near the end of the Pleistocene flooded lowlands and gradually separated the archipelago from surrounding lands. The process did not occur everywhere at once. Passages opened between Kyushu and the Ryukyu chain, between northern Kyushu and the Korean peninsula, and later between Honshu and Hokkaido. The shallow northern route between Hokkaido and Sakhalin remained available longer than the deeper southern crossings.

Southern, western, and northern corridors did not bring the same animals, people, or techniques at the same time. As the sea rose, habitats contracted, migration routes shifted, and water became both boundary and road. The archipelago emerged gradually from a continental margin rather than appearing at one moment as a finished island world.

Oriental elephants were followed by Naumann elephants, giant deer, and other large mammals entering through western routes, while mammoths moved south from Siberia into Hokkaido but apparently did not reach Honshu. Bones and teeth from the Inland Sea and Lake Nojiri preserve this history beside species that endured, including brown bears and Japanese deer.

In the Kanto plain, deposits from Hakone and Akagi formed the Tama, Shimosueyoshi, Musashino, and Tachikawa loams. These layers created fertile soils, but they also became an unusually clear archive of climate, fauna, and human occupation.

paragraphs.text: Clear stratification in the southern Kanto plain allows archaeologists to distinguish successive cultural stages beginning about thirty thousand years ago. Claims for substantially earlier occupation, once associated with sites such as Babadan and Zazaragi, require secure geology, unmistakably manufactured artifacts, and reliable dates. The decisive recognition of a Paleolithic presence came at Iwajuku in Gunma Prefecture, where stone artifacts were found beneath the familiar Jomon layers in 1947 and excavated in 1949. Human occupation could no longer be assumed to begin with pottery.

The Kanto plain offered a particularly favorable setting. Five major rivers, abundant springs, gravel beds rich in stone, distant mountain shelter, and mixed plant and animal life made repeated year-round occupation possible despite volcanic activity.

As warming followed, vegetation thickened, oaks expanded, and plant foods became more important while many large animals declined. Sites became larger and more numerous, refined projectile points appeared, and clusters of fire-blackened stones show that heated-stone cooking formed part of camp life.

paragraphs.text: People entered through widely separated corridors. The Korean route probably carried many early arrivals, while southern connections remained open and the far north became habitable only late in the sequence. Human bones attributed to this age are fragmentary and often disputed. The lost Akashi pelvic bone, the remains from Kannon-do and Hijiri-dake, and other finds show how little can be said securely about the appearance of the earliest inhabitants. The stone record is far stronger than the skeletal one.

Subalpine forests retreated, animals moved toward cooler ground, and hunters followed them into uplands, caves, and rock shelters. Large, slow species disappeared, while deer, wild boar, raccoon-dogs, hares, badgers, and other adaptable animals became the main game of later Jomon communities.

The bow and arrow appeared most clearly in northern and central hunting zones, where smaller and faster animals demanded lighter projectiles. Pottery appeared earliest in the south, where difficult subsistence conditions encouraged new ways of boiling plants, storing food, and carrying water. Both developments can be understood as local responses to changing environments, though the wider networks around them remain open to study.

Earlier layers contain spearpoints and the bones of deer, boar, bear, and monkey, while later layers add arrowheads and smaller animals such as otters, rabbits, flying squirrels, and birds. Fukui, Sempukuji, and Iwashita yielded small, low-fired vessels with round bases and simple raised or impressed decoration. It also supported storage and longer residence near nut forests and other seasonal resources. Microblades continued in Kyushu and connected the archipelago with northern Asia, where similar tools ranged through Sakhalin and Siberia. By the end of this transition, older mobile lifeways had not vanished, but the material basis of Jomon settlement had begun to form.

sections.title: Naming Jomon and the First Coastal Communities

paragraphs.text: The word Jomon means cord pattern. It arose from Edward Morse's description of pottery excavated at the Omori shell mounds in 1877 and gradually came to name the long period in which such ceramics were made. Yamanouchi Sugao later arranged Jomon pottery into Earliest, Early, Middle, Late, and Latest stages, with an added incipient phase for the pottery that preceded full Jomon lifeways. The sequence remains useful, though regional developments overlap and no stage lasted equally everywhere.

Bays, river mouths, tidal pools, and inlets offered shellfish even in winter, while fish supplemented declining terrestrial game. At Natsushima in Kanto, oysters, warm-water clams, freshwater fish, and changing marine species show a shoreline moving inland as the sea rose. Earlier settlements were flooded, and communities withdrew to higher ground.

A man buried at Hirasaka stood about one hundred sixty-three centimeters tall, but his teeth and bones record severe wear, childhood malnutrition, and early aging. paragraphs.text: During the Early Jomon, warming continued and the sea advanced deep into low valleys. Some Kanto settlements that are now far inland once stood near tidal water, while the Inland Sea opened fully and separated Shikoku and Kyushu from Honshu. Shell mounds preserve freshwater and marine clams, oysters, deer, boar, flying squirrels, and other animals, but the middle of the stage brought a striking rise in population.

Pit dwellings became more substantial, with inner posts, pitched roofs, drainage ditches, and eventually interior hearths. At Minabori in Yokohama, successive houses preserved the same broad arc around a communal space, suggesting that the village plan outlasted individual buildings. Storage pits lined with alternating leaves and nuts protected food and allowed only a small portion to be exposed at one time.

The climate remained warm, but altitude offered cooler summers, abundant springs, mixed forests, game, and access to obsidian. paragraphs.text: The economy rested on several overlapping harvests. Horse chestnuts came first, followed by chestnuts, acorns, and walnuts, while yams, lily bulbs, bracken, arrowroot, mushrooms, and other plants broadened the diet. Bitter acorns and horse chestnuts required prolonged leaching, which helps explain the importance of springs. Charred breadlike remains from Idojiri suggest that starches were processed, steamed, and stored for winter. Whether this amounted to agriculture remains debated, but long residence almost certainly encouraged selection, transplanting, and management of useful plants.

paragraphs.text: Middle Jomon pottery grew larger and more varied. Upright jars, bowls, steamers, cups, lamps, and ritual vessels appeared beside one another, while mountain potters built thick walls with modeled ridges, handles, and dramatic rims. Katsusaka wares flourished in the highlands, Otamadai pottery in the lowlands and coastal plain, and later Kasori E vessels favored dense oblique cord marking.

Because mica sources were limited, the wide distribution of these vessels implies movement of clay, pots, or potters. Katsusaka settlements stood near springs and the routes leading toward obsidian sources south of Lake Suwa. The venomous mamushi, with its hibernation, shedding skin, and dangerous bite, may have supported associations with death and renewal. Clay figurines became far more numerous, many emphasizing breasts and hips, and a few bearing coiled snakes. Large pots were placed beneath entrances or inverted over infant remains, sometimes after their bases had been removed or pierced. Heavy digging, grinding, building, and food preparation shaped bones and teeth, while high carbohydrate consumption left a clear dental signature. Earlier attempts to assign particular skeletal changes rigidly to male or female work require caution. What remains unmistakable is the physical cost of maintaining a settled highland economy.

sections.title: The End of the Highland World

paragraphs.text: Around 2400 BC, repeated rains appear to have damaged the nut harvests on which the highland settlements depended. Communities left many mountain sites and moved toward lower river valleys and the coast, where marine foods offered a different security. In Chubu, the recorded number of settlements fell from nearly three thousand in the Middle Jomon to fewer than one thousand in the Late stage and about two hundred fifty in the Latest.

Regions that had held few Middle Jomon settlements, including parts of the Kinki, Chugoku, Shikoku, Kyushu, and the north, received larger populations. Kasori E pottery spread farther than earlier highland styles, and erased cord marking became widely shared. Migration weakened some regional boundaries while creating new combinations of local practice.

sections.title: Late Jomon Coasts and Seasonal Life

paragraphs.text: Many Late Jomon communities occupied sheltered bays, river mouths, and coastal terraces. Their refuse formed immense shell mounds, some more than one hundred meters long, from Hokkaido and northern Honshu to Kanto, the Inland Sea, Kyushu, and islands farther south. The rugged Japan Sea coast preserves far fewer.

paragraphs.text: Shell growth rings suggest that clamming was concentrated in spring, with a smaller season in late summer. Fishing expanded from inshore waters to tuna, bonito, salmon, trout, and porpoises according to region. Dugout canoes carried crews into deeper water, while hunting remained important for deer and boar. The year followed a broad rhythm of shellfish in spring, fishing in summer, nuts in autumn, and hunting in winter.

These have been interpreted as houses of ritual leaders or communal ceremonial places, but their plans do not determine the answer.

paragraphs.text: The heavy chipped axes of the Middle Jomon almost disappeared, while smaller ground and polished tools became more common. Small arrowheads were used with simple bows, and some may have been tipped with aconite poison, though direct proof is limited. Pottery became thinner and more controlled, with restrained linear decoration that followed the vessel's shape. In Kyushu, dark polished Goryo wares departed sharply from cord-marked traditions and may reflect distant continental connections. Mat impressions reveal developed basketry, while softened mulberry bark and woven plant fiber probably provided clothing and rainwear.

At Kainohana in Chiba, a long-lived settlement produced stone phalli, stone swords, clay disks, plaques, and figurines, many of them concentrated in a shared central area. Two houses contained smaller groups of the same objects and may have belonged to ritual specialists, though no office can be recovered from the remains. The later, smaller community used the common space more intensively, showing that population decline did not entail ritual decline.

Northern examples sometimes show squatting bodies, which have been connected with childbirth, flexed burial, healing, or sympathetic magic. Their exact meanings remain uncertain, but repeated handling, breaking, and deposition show that they belonged to enduring domestic and communal practices.

The circles may have joined seasonal salmon gatherings, burial, exchange, and ceremony. Ordinary houses are scarce nearby, making their separation from daily residence more secure than any proposed calendar.

paragraphs.text: Craft and exchange likewise became more visible. Some settlements held more fishhooks, stone tools, or unfinished objects than their inhabitants appear to have needed. Coastal communities exchanged salt, dried fish, shell products, and seaweed for obsidian, bone, horn, and inland foods, while asphalt from a few Akita sources traveled widely through Tohoku. These routes joined communities without requiring permanent markets or professional merchants.

paragraphs.text: The Latest Jomon is conventionally placed between about 1000 and 300 BC, though the boundary is least secure in Kyushu, where rice cultivation had already begun. Settlement contracted sharply across the archipelago, and more than half of known sites lay in Tohoku. Northern communities continued to draw on horse chestnuts, walnuts, deer, salmon, and other marine foods, sometimes while managing useful plants and disturbing nearby forests.

Wet sites preserve a richer domestic world of bowls, cups, baskets, combs, and ritual objects. Small vessels were polished, burnished, or lacquered, and household members may have possessed individual cups or bowls.

Applied over red pigment to wood and pottery, it protected surfaces and created a valued finish, as seen in combs, baskets, and a ceremonial sword. Hollow figurines, including the famous goggle-eyed forms, also belong to this vigorous northern ritual world. Their identities are uncertain, but their technical assurance is not.

sections.title: Rice at the End of Jomon

paragraphs.text: Kyushu's population rose after the Late Jomon migrations, placing greater pressure on local resources while proximity to the continent opened new possibilities. Rice impressions have been reported on Latest Jomon pottery, especially in northern Kyushu, and rice pollen appears with weeds associated with forest clearance. At Itazuke, a paddy surface linked to Yusu pottery preserved the footprints of adults and a child working in wet ground. The discovery made a clean boundary between Jomon and Yayoi impossible.

paragraphs.text: Rice was not the only crop under consideration. Millet, barley, wheat, and beans have been identified in late Jomon or early transitional contexts, though some identifications and dates remain debated. The essential change was not the sudden arrival of one grain, but the growth of a mixed productive economy in which managed plants, dry fields, and wet paddies joined older fishing, hunting, and gathering.

paragraphs.text: The relation between Jomon populations and later Ainu was once treated too simply. Northern Latest Jomon communities contributed to the ancestry and culture of later northern peoples, but Jomon society across the archipelago was never one homogeneous population. Skeletal studies show both continuity and regional difference, while the historical labels Emishi and Ezo belong to later political encounters. No single line can turn the entire Jomon world into one later people.

The transition to Yayoi was therefore regional, cumulative, and uneven.

paragraphs.text: The name Yayoi comes from a district near the University of Tokyo where pottery unlike Jomon wares was found in the late nineteenth century. Its significance remained uncertain for decades, and the period acquired a clear archaeological identity only through later excavation, especially at Toro. Yayoi roughly overlaps the Han dynasties of China, but it began earlier and ended later than that continental frame.

paragraphs.text: Older explanations opposed foreign invasion to indigenous development. Neither is sufficient. Rice agriculture, metallurgy, and associated tools entered through northern Kyushu over several centuries. They came from the Korean peninsula and eastern China, but existing communities adopted them rather than receiving them through one conquest. The small population of Latest Jomon Kyushu made immigration important, yet no archaeological evidence supports total replacement.

paragraphs.text: Romantic claims that Xu Fu brought rice and metal in a single expedition fail against the different chronologies of those technologies. The opposite claim that southern Jomon communities independently domesticated rice and invented bronze and iron ignores the continental origins of the plants and techniques. The transition was neither an isolated invention nor a complete transplantation. It was a long process of migration, teaching, exchange, and local recombination.

The collapse of Zhou authority, the unification of Qin, the expansion of Han, and the creation of the Lelang commandery in northern Korea altered the routes through which people and objects reached the archipelago. Maritime travel from Korea through Tsushima and Iki connected northern Kyushu to a broader East Asian field of trade and diplomacy.

Ongagawa wares spread from northern Kyushu along the Inland Sea to the Kinki and Tokai, while Yusu pottery remains difficult to separate from the earliest Yayoi forms. paragraphs.text: Yayoi communities did not seek entirely new landscapes. Large sites in Chiba and Nagano contain both Jomon and Yayoi houses, showing that old settlements could be reoccupied or transformed as economic priorities changed. Burial practices also crossed the conventional boundary, with jars and circular pits continuing in eastern regions before square-moated graves became common.

paragraphs.text: The earliest rice suited a temperate zone extending from the lower Yangtze region toward southern Korea. Short-grained rice could be dried, toasted, and stored compactly, but it demanded protection from damp, insects, and rodents. Later communities raised storehouses above the ground and used wooden pounders to prepare grain and fertilizing material.

paragraphs.text: Itazuke lay beside the Mikasa River in northern Kyushu and was occupied in the Earliest Jomon, the Latest Jomon, and again during Early and Middle Yayoi. Its threshold character appears in pottery that is difficult to classify cleanly, beside unmistakable Yayoi storage jars, wooden field stakes, and a long ditch that may have carried water or defended the settlement.

Stone reaping knives, polished axes, and spindle whorls belonged to the new economy, while iron tools must have shaped much of the wood even though no iron scraps were found in the earliest levels. The absence of house pits may mean that dwellings stood on the surface, where damp ground made sunken floors uncomfortable.

It contained sixty-three jar burials and fifty rectangular pits, at least twelve of which probably held wooden coffins. Children were usually placed in single jars, while adults could be enclosed in two joined vessels. The dead occupied a defined space apart from fields and storage.

The practice became extremely common in Middle Yayoi northern Kyushu, with some cemeteries containing hundreds or even thousands of jars. By Late Yayoi, simpler pits for bodies wrapped in mats became more usual.

Large jars were sometimes covered by heavy stones in dolmen-like arrangements, while stone cists appeared in western Honshu, Kyushu, and the islands of the Korean strait. These forms rarely contained rich goods, but they placed the dead within a wider maritime tradition.

paragraphs.text: Doigahama in Yamaguchi reveals more complex distinctions. Most bodies lay extended with their heads toward the east, but a small group of stone cists occupied the center and alone contained jasper and shell ornaments. Men, women, and children were distributed unevenly through different parts of the cemetery, and tooth modification remained common. Age, sex, kinship, marriage, origin, and rank may all have shaped the pattern, though no single explanation accounts for it.

paragraphs.text: Square-moated graves became especially important in the Kinki and neighboring regions. A wooden coffin or burial lay within a square or rectangular space defined by a ditch, sometimes with additional bodies arranged around it. These graves remained closer to the Yayoi practice of burial below ground than to the monumental mounds that followed, yet they formed part of the architectural ancestry of later tombs.

Large concentrations at Ihara, Mikumo, and Sugu reveal communities able to accumulate continental prestige goods and local weapons. Such wealth has encouraged attempts to identify the region with Yamatai, but the finds establish political importance more securely than a specific name.

paragraphs.text: The cemeteries mark an early rise in social height. Objects once acquired through exchange became personal treasures and burial signs, while specialized potters produced enormous jars beyond ordinary household needs. Difference was no longer expressed only through age or ritual role. It was becoming material, accumulative, and inheritable.

sections.title: Iron and the Transformation of Work

paragraphs.text: A few objects from late Jomon and Early Yayoi contexts have been proposed as the first iron in the archipelago, but the earliest secure examples belong roughly to the second century BC. An iron sword from a wooden coffin near Fukuoka and blade fragments from Kumamoto stand among the oldest finds. Most early pieces were probably imported, and corrosion has erased much of the original record.

paragraphs.text: The first iron objects reflected continental casting traditions. Forging later spread with Han technological influence and was better suited to the smaller workshops of the archipelago. The sharp rise in Middle Yayoi iron cannot be explained by imported finished tools alone. Local smithing, the search for ore, and the recycling of metal must have expanded.

paragraphs.text: Iron may have come from Korean sources, but river sands and limonite also offered local material. Primitive furnaces reported in Oita and Miyazaki could refine small batches, though their identification and date require caution. The central change was the movement from possessing iron to knowing how to work it.

paragraphs.text: By Late Yayoi, iron entered farming, carpentry, fishing, and war. Plows, hoes, sickles, axes, adzes, chisels, planes, hooks, arrowheads, spearheads, swords, and halberds extended the reach of labor. The metal remained unevenly distributed, with few surviving pieces in Kanto and almost none in Tohoku, but absence must be weighed against rapid corrosion.

paragraphs.text: Wet sites preserve the wooden world shaped by these edges. Excavators have recovered rakes, hoes, loom parts, fire drills, bowls, stools, painted shields, carved birds, human effigies, paddy clogs, and even the body of a koto. In the Kinki, pottery, carved wood, and bronze shared the flowing-water pattern known as ryusui. Iron did not replace wood. It made a new precision in wood possible.

paragraphs.text: Toro stood beside the Abe River in present-day Shizuoka. A catastrophic flood ended one phase of the settlement and aligned broken timbers with the flow of the water, preserving the clearest known plan of a mature Yayoi farming village. Few valuables remained, perhaps because the inhabitants escaped with warning or returned to recover them. No iron tools survived, though thousands of regular wooden slats show that iron had shaped the site.

paragraphs.text: More than fifty paddies occupied about seventy thousand square meters. Ditches, sluices, and wells directed water through the fields, and raised storehouses protected the harvest from damp, insects, and rodents. These buildings stood on heavy posts above the earth and embodied some of the settlement's most advanced carpentry. Their form may stand behind later elevated residences and sacred buildings, though Toro alone cannot establish a direct line from granary to palace or shrine.

paragraphs.text: Houses stood over shallow oval pits on slightly higher ground. Heavy posts rested on buried plates in the soft soil, while thatched roofs, drains, and earthen benches answered a landscape where water was both necessary and dangerous. Regional plans differed, and some southern houses lacked hearths, perhaps because of dampness and warm conditions.

paragraphs.text: Much of the village economy appears to have been collective. Tools were stored together, one granary served several houses, and dwellings stood too close for every household to dry grain independently. Ditches had to be opened, cleared, and repaired according to a common rhythm. The management of ordinary necessity created leadership before any title is known.

paragraphs.text: Population growth sent branch settlements toward higher ground, where wells opened new areas to cultivation. Rice remained central, but millet, beans, peas, barley, wheat, peaches, and gathered fruits broadened the food base. The agricultural village coordinated paddies, dry fields, storage, fishing, and wild resources rather than narrowing life to one grain.

paragraphs.text: Chinese accounts describe wars among the communities of Wa, and archaeology reveals weapons, defensive works, violent injuries, and settlements abandoned in crisis. Stone tools once used in hunting were enlarged or redirected toward combat, especially from the eastern Inland Sea into the Kinki. At Doigahama, a stone arrowhead struck a skull; at Nejiko, a bronze point remained embedded in a woman's head; and several bodies at Yoshinogari were headless.

Santonodai stood on a plateau above Yokohama Bay, enclosed by a ditch and supplied by rice fields near springs below the eastern slope. Houses were rebuilt there from Middle Yayoi into the Yamato period, turning a defensible place into a crowded settlement across generations.

Later dwellings held storage pits, and deep shafts at the edge of the plateau may have stored grain for common use. The defended village joined agriculture, collective reserves, and coercive power on one height.

paragraphs.text: Warfare distinguished allies from enemies and tightened obligations within communities. Competition for land, water, ore, and routes encouraged the formation of larger political centers, particularly around the Kinki and Inland Sea. Growth in production did not bring peace. It raised the value of what could be controlled.

paragraphs.text: Bronze and iron acquired different social careers. Iron entered ordinary production, while bronze concentrated in mirrors, ornaments, weapons, bells, and public ritual. Casting demanded trained artisans, controlled alloys, molds, and organized access to imported material, making bronze easier to supervise and harder to obtain. Its political force arose from scarcity, brilliance, sound, and controlled display.

paragraphs.text: Yayoi bronze finds form two broad zones. Weapons concentrate in northern Kyushu and the western Inland Sea, while bells concentrate from the eastern Inland Sea through the Kinki and into southern Tokai. The zones overlap around Kibi, whose communities controlled the routes between Kyushu and the Kinki. Distribution reveals contact and rivalry, though it does not prove one continuous war between two fixed blocs.

Later weapons became longer, wider, and thinner until many were no longer practical. The form of violence had been converted into a ceremonial sign.

Groups of swords, spearheads, and halberds were placed together, sometimes arranged by size and perhaps associated with fields, boundaries, or communal protection. The suggestion that they were periodically unearthed and reburied remains possible but unproved. What is secure is that communities removed large quantities of metal from use in deliberate acts.

sections.title: Bronze Bells and the Craft of Casting

paragraphs.text: The earliest bells were small and resembled Korean horse bells. For a time, scholars assumed that Kyushu imported them without casting them, but mold fragments and workshop debris in Fukuoka and Saga overturned that geography. At Yasunagata, a used bell mold lay with spearhead molds, copper slag, and refined tin, joining several stages of metalworking in one place.

paragraphs.text: Early Inland Sea bells were technically uncertain. Trapped gases scarred their surfaces, flaws were patched, and a few examples carried crude lines resembling faces. By about the second century AD, casters produced sharper relief, cleaner flanges, and more controlled panels. During the third century, bells became taller, thinner, and increasingly standardized.

paragraphs.text: About one bell in ten bears small pictures in thread-like relief. Animals, fish, insects, storehouses, ritual figures, rice pounding, fishing, and hunting with dogs appear within ordered panels. The scenes may have accompanied planting and harvest ceremonies, but their words are lost. The images show which acts of subsistence and ritual were worthy of sacred metal.

Several sets include objects from the Kinki, and a nearly complete mold from Ibaraki in Osaka strengthens the case for major foundries around Osaka and Nara. The same workshop also produced molds for curved beads and equipment for bellows. Crafts were concentrated, while finished objects traveled far beyond the place of manufacture.

The widening distribution of bells may reflect expanding Kinki influence, exchange among allied communities, or both. Technical standardization and political consolidation were moving together, though neither can be reduced to the other.

At Sakuragaoka above Kobe, fourteen bells and seven halberds were concealed together on a wooded ridge. The ceremony is unrecoverable, but carrying, arranging, and surrendering so much metal made burial an act of exceptional public weight.

paragraphs.text: The quantity of bronze raises the problem of supply. A later chronicle celebrated the discovery of copper in Musashi in 708 through the era name Wado. If substantial local copper had not been available earlier, Yayoi workshops depended on ore, ingots, finished objects, or scrap moving across the sea and then inland. The hundreds of surviving bells and weapons represent only part of the metal once circulating.

A mirror, vessel, or weapon could be recast as a bell or ceremonial blade suited to a different political and ritual world. Such translation required technical knowledge and authorities able to secure, protect, and distribute scarce material.

The tested bells had broadly consistent alloys, and the oldest examples aligned with Korean material, while many others corresponded to Former Han or later Chinese sources. The results support extensive importation but cannot identify the merchants, ports, or agreements behind each movement.

Repeated heating could alter the alloy while the metal retained an isotopic trace of its origin. The Yayoi bronze economy rested on maritime acquisition, local transformation, and political control.

paragraphs.text: The fullest external description of late Yayoi society appears in the Chinese history conventionally called the Wei zhi, compiled in the late third century. It describes Wa as a field of many countries, some in direct contact with Chinese commanderies, and names Yamatai as the strongest federation after a period of war. The account is invaluable because it is external and comparatively early, but it is shaped by Chinese diplomatic categories, imperfect reports, and a taste for large round numbers.

paragraphs.text: Yamatai was ruled by Himiko, a woman whose authority was represented as both sacred and political. She lived in seclusion, was served by many women, guarded by armed men, and communicated through one brother who assisted in government. The numbers may be conventional, but the structure of secluded ritual authority joined to an administrative intermediary is historically significant.

Men of status were said to have several wives. Professional abstainers accompanied travelers and could be killed if misfortune suggested that they had broken their vows. Divination used burned bones, mourning lasted ten days, and burial took place in a single coffin.

paragraphs.text: After Himiko's death, a male successor failed to restore order. Peace returned only when a thirteen-year-old girl was placed in authority. Himiko was said to have been buried in a mound about one hundred meters across with a thousand attendants sacrificed at her death. The scale and immolation figure cannot be accepted literally without corroboration, but the account firmly places female ritual rule, succession crisis, and monumental burial within the political imagination of third-century Wa.

These first stages can be placed with reasonable confidence. Beyond them, the account gives travel in days by sea and land rather than dependable distances, and the resulting geography has sustained centuries of debate.

paragraphs.text: One influential reading favors a destination in central Japan and treats Yamatai as a Chinese rendering of Yamato. It argued that the long journey beyond northern Kyushu was unnecessary if the destination lay nearby. Other scholars have read the same directions differently, and the location remains disputed. The record securely reveals a route of maritime contact and a powerful federation; it does not securely fix that federation on a modern map.

paragraphs.text: The dispute became entangled with imperial genealogy. Himiko could not be fitted easily into the lengthened male succession of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, and attempts to identify her with the ruler Jingu never resolved the contradictions. Moving Yamatai away from Yamato offered one way to keep the Chinese queen outside the imperial line. The controversy therefore concerns not only distance and direction, but the relation between external testimony and later court memory.

The traditional Yamato line places Jingu and Ojin within received court succession, showing why the attempted identification of Himiko with Jingu created chronological and genealogical difficulties.

paragraphs.text: Archaeology confirms several customs described by the Chinese account without proving the location of Yamatai. Burned shoulder bones show divination, simple wooden coffins differ from the nested coffins of wealthy Chinese burials, and the scarcity of chopsticks supports the report that food was eaten by hand. Loom parts and surviving cloth show the production of narrow textiles from silk and plant fibers. External testimony and material evidence meet most securely in ordinary practices rather than in the debated name of a capital.

sections.title: Rank, Trade, and the Fabric of Society

paragraphs.text: Chinese descriptions of deference and graded titles agree with archaeological signs of social difference. At Tano in Osaka, larger houses were associated with wooden coffins and grave goods, while smaller dwellings stood near poorer jar burials. Beads, bronze bracelets, nonlocal jasper, and a painted coffin distinguished a few dead from others buried without possessions. The exact social categories are unknown, but equality is no longer a plausible description.

paragraphs.text: Bronze and textiles may both have strengthened hierarchy. Access to imported metal, skilled workshops, fine cloth, and the routes through which they moved could be controlled and redistributed. Leadership was expressed not only through weapons or ritual, but through the ability to gather goods from distant regions and place them in chosen hands.

paragraphs.text: Trade linked the archipelago at many scales. Rice appeared in northern sites where it may not have grown, iron reached regions without local ore, and salt-producing settlements made more than their own inhabitants required. Stone reapers from Tateiwa and polished axes from Imayama traveled through northern Kyushu, while wooden tools moved between forest margins and farming plains near Osaka. A man buried at Tateiwa wore fourteen bracelets made from shells whose nearest source lay in the Ryukyu Islands.

As settlements spread inland, the demand for salt, tools, and imported materials increased. Exchange became part of the structure through which villages survived and leaders distinguished themselves.

paragraphs.text: Older linguistic scholarship treated Japanese as fundamentally related to northern languages, with additional southern elements already present by Yayoi times. Such claims belong to an older linguistic framework and cannot be accepted as settled history. What the historical record does show is that communication across the Korean strait did not erase linguistic difference. By later centuries, interpreters were needed even within immigrant craft communities.

paragraphs.text: Human remains offer firmer, though still incomplete, evidence for population change. About a thousand Yayoi skeletons were known from southwestern Japan, many preserved in burial jars. Early Yayoi people in northern and western Kyushu were on average somewhat taller than Jomon predecessors but otherwise often similar. The evidence does not support a single invading population replacing everyone already present.

paragraphs.text: Differences became clearer toward the end of Yayoi. Faces grew flatter in many samples, stature and skull form varied by region, and nutrition affected growth, teeth, and longevity. Some older studies divided weapon-burying and bell-burying populations too sharply by skull shape. Regional ancestry mattered, but food, labor, disease, and marriage could transform bodies within a few generations.

paragraphs.text: Population rose dramatically. Older estimates counted more than ten thousand Yayoi sites and placed the total population at roughly six hundred thousand, several times that of Latest Jomon. The figures are approximate, but the direction is secure. Rice agriculture and mixed farming supported denser settlement, while stable occupation was especially marked in the Kinki. The Osaka-Nara region offered fertile plains, protected basins, and access to inland and maritime routes. Its later political importance rested on this long accumulation of people and place.

paragraphs.text: The chronicles place the expedition of Jimmu within a world of competing Yayoi chieftains. He travels from southern Kyushu through the Inland Sea, overcomes resistance in Kibi, fails to enter the Kinki directly from Osaka, and reaches the Nara basin by circling to the east. The account is not a securely dated campaign, but its geography reflects enduring political facts: the strategic weight of Kibi, the strength of the Kinki approaches, and the attraction of the lower Nara basin.

paragraphs.text: At moments of danger, Jimmu seeks counsel from kami, performs abstinence and sacrifice, and resumes the advance. The story makes ritual mediation inseparable from command. Chinese descriptions of shamanic rulers, archaeological evidence for warfare, and the rise of a strong third-century center in the Kinki do not prove the chronicle narrative, but they make its political world intelligible.

paragraphs.text: The later court used Jimmu to express a foundation that joined conquest, migration, and divine authorization. His genealogy belongs to sacred memory, while the growth of Kinki power belongs to archaeology. The two witnesses should be heard together without being mistaken for the same voice.

paragraphs.text: At Kojindani in Shimane, a road project uncovered a cache of three hundred fifty-eight bronze swords, sixteen spearheads, and six bells. The number of swords exceeded the total then known from the rest of the archipelago. They lay on a slope above the Hikawa plain, near the Hii River, Lake Shinji, ancient burial mounds, and the wider sacred landscape of Izumo.

They were placed in four ordered rows within an oblong pit. Most points faced east, while a dark organic layer above them may preserve a cloth covering and nearby postholes suggest a light structure.

paragraphs.text: Court mythology sends Susa no O, the brother of Amaterasu, from the heavenly community to the bank of the Hii River. There he kills the eight-headed serpent and establishes himself in Izumo. His descendant Okuni Nushi becomes the principal rival of the heavenly line and must surrender authority before Yamato's sacred order can begin.

The stories are strongest as evidence for how later Yamato arranged its relation to rival sacred centers.

paragraphs.text: In the settlement narrated by the chronicles, Okuni Nushi receives a great palace and continuing honor in exchange for withdrawal from political rule. Izumo retains religious responsibility, while the descendants of Amaterasu claim government. Conquest is recast as a division of sacred and political authority. The special oath later required of Izumo's governor and the continuing importance of the Great Shrine preserved the memory that this submission was never ordinary.

paragraphs.text: Northern Kyushu formed another center, rich in bronze weapons and continental connections. One older reconstruction connected this spear tradition with the sun-spear imagery of myth and imagined an eastward movement of male chieftains into regions associated with bells and female sacred authority. The correspondence is suggestive but too exact to be secure. What can be seen is recombination: weapons, bells, mirrors, immigrant techniques, regional rites, and expanding alliances were gathered into new symbols of rule.

paragraphs.text: Himiko shows that female ritual authority could stand at the center of a third-century federation. The Yamato chronicles likewise placed Amaterasu, a female deity, above the ancestral order of the ruling house. Yet they organized earthly succession through an extended male genealogy whose earliest reigns lack independent dates, acts, or inscriptions.

paragraphs.text: Later compilers had reason to enlarge the antiquity and continuity of the male line, while later historians sharpened it further. This made Himiko difficult to place and encouraged both her identification with Jingu and the removal of Yamatai from Yamato. Neither solution should be treated as established. Female shamans, brothers, male chieftains, mothers, and sacred ancestors all participated in early authority. The evidence does not describe a simple passage from matriarchy to patriarchy.

The competing dates assigned to his death are uncertain, but he is often treated as the earliest ruler around whom substantial Yamato memory gathers.

paragraphs.text: A large keyhole tomb south of Tenri has traditionally been assigned to Sujin. The personal identification cannot be proved, but the tomb form belongs to the late third or early fourth century, when monumental keyhole mounds appeared in the Nara basin and spread through political networks. Sujin therefore stands at the boundary between traditional genealogy and the archaeological horizon of the Kofun age.

paragraphs.text: Claims for occupation before thirty-five thousand BC remain disputed, but from about thirty thousand years ago the Paleolithic record becomes widespread and regionally varied. Mobile communities adapted stone technology to changing animals, plants, climates, and volcanic landscapes. Rapid warming and rising seas then transformed subsistence, and pottery, the bow, coastal foods, and shell mounds formed the basis of early Jomon life.

paragraphs.text: Jomon history was not a pause before agriculture. Early warming supported a great rise in coastal population, while Middle Jomon communities built large highland settlements around springs, forest harvests, storage, craft, and the central hearth. When repeated rains weakened that economy, people moved toward coasts and lower valleys, carrying pottery, ritual practice, and exchange into new regional combinations.

paragraphs.text: By Latest Jomon, the largest concentrations lay in the north, while northern Kyushu entered an agricultural transition. Rice cultivation began before the old pottery sequence had ended. Wet fields, dry crops, fishing, and gathering coexisted, and immigrants joined existing populations rather than replacing them in one movement.

paragraphs.text: Iron and bronze arrived through continental and peninsular connections, but communities within the archipelago selected, copied, enlarged, recast, and ritualized them differently. Agriculture supported larger villages, storage, specialization, and stronger claims over land and water. Moats, weapons, wounded bodies, and Chinese reports show that the same growth intensified conflict.

paragraphs.text: Federations emerged in northern Kyushu, along the Inland Sea, in Izumo, and in the Kinki. Weapons and mirrors were prominent in the west, bells farther east, though the zones overlapped. By the third century, the Nara basin sustained a center able to gather agricultural wealth, ritual authority, military force, and continental connections. The Yamato state did not arise from an empty country or an inevitable national destiny. It emerged from the long convergence of regional societies, and its new scale of power became visible in the immense mounds of the Kofun age.
